projects.name: Tanzania Food Systems Resilience Programme - Horticulture (TFSRP-H)
projects.description: The Tanzania Food Systems Resilience Program – Horticulture (TFSRP-H) strengthens food systems by improving agricultural service delivery, promoting climate-resilient technologies, and enhancing fiscal performance. As part of a USD 2.75 billion regional initiative financed by the World Bank, the program receives USD 40 million in co-financing from IFAD to focus specifically on youth, horticulture, and access to finance. In response to the President of Tanzania’s call for targeted youth support under the Building a Better Tomorrow – Youth in Agriculture (BBT-YIA) initiative, the project aims to establish at least one profitable youth-led agribusiness in each of the country’s 12,000 villages. It targets young women and men aged 18–35 engaged in horticulture, supporting them through seed systems, extension services, research, and postharvest infrastructure such as packhouses, storage facilities, processing plants, and tissue culture labs. Youth participate as seed multipliers, producers, technicians, agri-input specialists, lead farmers, and market information providers. The project builds youth capacity through agribusiness hubs, improves access to productive assets via financial literacy and youth-focused services, creates decent jobs on and off the farm, promotes youth leadership in farmer groups, and supports digital and innovative solutions for youth engagement. TFSRP-H targets 100% youth participation and integrates IFAD’s expertise in supporting smallholder farmers, with a strong focus on youth, gender, climate resilience, and nutrition. By promoting climate-smart practices and increasing the supply of fresh horticultural products, the project contributes to both environmental sustainability and improved household nutrition.

projects.name: Productivity and resilience of dairy production systems (CSDTP Component 1)
projects.description:
The Climate Smart Dairy Transformation Programme (CSDTP); A Climate smart livestock (CSL) development combines increasing productivity and climate change adaptation of livestock development with climate change mitigation by reducing livestock-related Greenhouse Gas (GHG) emissions. CSL is mainstreamed throughout C-SDTP’s interventions which include;  Animal health, breed choice, fodders and farmer management are the cornerstones for both resilience and productivity increase (which also results in lower GHG emission intensities). Productivity increase, rather than only production or yield increase, needs high management knowledge and practices, as well as last mile services and increased animal health support. To achieve the levels of knowledge and technology adoption required, farmers first receive a L-FFS training, including Climate Smart and One Health priorities, which is then followed by a successful dairy management coaching trajectory. The latter is an innovation for the Tanzanian context and a doorstep service. This will be piloted and researched during the project, before being scaled up for impact. At the same time, the animal health service infrastructure needs to be rolled out to reach on-farm (also a doorstep service) and must beside the usual preventive and therapeutic services also include health issues affecting production and human health (zoonotic diseases and AMR). Private veterinary care and laboratory services therefore need outreach to the farms and inform and support farmer animal health and management decision making to improve both productivity (and revenues and GHGe reductions) and One Health. These elements combined further strengthen alignment of C-SDTP with the food systems agenda, and consequently the programme’s alignment with the country’s COSOP and Tanzania’s policy objectives. 
Subcomponent 1.1: Capacity building, social mobilization and asset building which involves i) building production assets of 8600 (600 in Zanzibar and 8000 in mainland)  vulnerable households through provision of dairy cows and cowshed construction support ii) Biogas generation from cowsheds will be installed at the household  iii) livestock Farmers Field Schools (L-FFS) to improve farm management practices and increase production, productivity and resilience 58 000 farmers (40% female, 20% youth, 3% PWDs, and 2 320 groups) will benefit. At first, the project will focus on the development of a specific curriculum on climate smart dairy production, and training of master trainers, who will then train the facilitators. The curriculum will cover deal with fodder and feed management, including fodder harvesting and conservation, reproductive management, health management including One Health aspects and management of anti-microbials, climate adaptation, manure management and animal welfare. L-FFS will be monitored by public LEWs to enroll 58 000 farmers (40% female, 20% youth, 3% PWDs, and 2 320 groups). Cooperative members will also be prioritised, 
 32 000 cooperatives members, Gender Action Learning System (GALS) methodology will be implemented and intertwined with 1 000 L-FFS groups to address power relations and inequalities especially at household level (reaching 25 000 HHs). 
Subcomponent 2: Essential services for sustainable production this will include i) extension and veterinary services for poor farmers is for the most part currently ii)  Animal health laboratory services are essential for diagnostic, animal disease surveillance, particularly AMR stewardship and the national disease surveillance information system concerning trans boundary and zoonotic infectious diseases. Clinical and subclinical infections have a major impact on productivity and thus on GHG emission intensities. Therefore, detecting and preventing the spread and continuation of infectious diseases is essential for climate smart livestock development iii)  Breeding and genetic improvement aims at improving productivity while preserving resilience of livestock keeping systems by crossing indigenous and exotic breeds through AI. Indigenous breeds are a reservoir for resilience traits, making them more adaptive including to climate change, whereas improved breeds will add productive traits to the gene pool, increasing the offspring’s productivity (mitigating GHG emission intensities), iv)  Fodder seeds production and pasture availability will be supported through 5 resilient fodder seeds producers per district (110 in total), v)  enhancing availability of water for livestock will be supported at household and community level vi) Scaling of digitalization for improved productivity. Building on the animal registration supported by MLF as part of the animal registration and livestock traceability act of 2010, the Project will scale up and upgrade the Tanzania National Livestock Identification and Traceability System (TANLITS) to promote health and vaccinations tracking, disease control and traceability as well as enhance identification for ownership and enabling access to services such as finance, insurance, breeding, performance recording and productivity advisory to dairy farmers. The project will also scale up the M-kilimo application, including a Livestock Digital Call Centre providing advise on animal husbandry from extension workers, as well as other production services (connection to AI and Animal Health Service Providers) to be hosted by MLF in Tanzania Mainland vii)  Disease intelligence, vaccination campaigns and contingency fund: with regard to climate smart livestock development, animal health can significantly reduce emissions, leading to greater sustainability throughout global food systems and mitigating livestock’s contribution to climate change. Essential public missions such as disease surveillance and disease emergency preparedness and response will be strengthened viii) Applied research for climate-smart farm management will be undertaken to achieve, through farmers’ management adoption, the productivity and health levels needed to reduce GHG emission intensities including the adoption of good climate smart practices enhancing resilience. 

Dissemination of climate-smart innovations and nature-based solutions to improve productivity, climate resilience and reduce GHG emissions will include; i) Introduction, testing and dissemination of climate-resilient fodder varieties and technologies and promoting agroforestry systems, ii) Promotion of energy-efficient and GHG emission reduction technologies for production iii) Climate smart and One Health dairy management study led by ILRI in collaboration with TALIRI, ZALIRI and SUA, will be done with a subset of farmers having received L-FFS training. This study will document how successful the dairy coaching and advise concept to perform in the Tanzanian context to help both farmer and LEW/para-veterinarian to plan and implement management goals and thus improve productivity, health and adoption of technologies and innovations at the farms. The outcomes of this study will feed into the extension systems for scaling up and serve as a pilot for the research iv) Carbon trading and low carbon certification in the dairy sector, will eventually open opportunities to access carbon markets.

projects.name: Inclusive and climate-smart value chains, private investment, milk consumption and policy (CSDTP Component 2)
projects.description:
The project is organized in four subcomponents; Subcomponent 2.1: Organization of producers, milk aggregation and facilitation of productive alliances. Creation and strengthening of dairy producers’ groups and cooperatives: the project will provide all farmer groups and cooperatives involved in milk collection and aggregation MCCs/MCPs, initial training and continuous coaching services to improve their business management, financial literacy, governance, and leadership skills. This role willb entrusted to a qualified and experienced service provider (most likely an international NGO). Institutional support will also be provided to regional and national dairy farmers organizations. The Construction and rehabilitation of MCCs to potentially collect 300 000 liters of milk (200 per cent increase) by establishing 100 new MCCs with an average capacity of 3 000 liters. The Project will also rehabilitate 60% of the existing MCCs to improve their efficiency (including energetic), sanitary conditions and hygiene. The climate smart MCCs use renewable energy, reduce and recycle waste and wastewater, reduce post harvest losses of milk (also downstream) and are constructed of materials that are as climate and environment friendly as possible. Support to primary collection and milk transportation from farm to MCP/MCC to improve quantitative and qualitative supply of milk will be done by supporting milk transporters, focusing on youth, for them to access loans to finance motorcycles, milk cans, and can holders. Free basic milk testing equipment will be provided with capacity building on milk hygiene. Hence, waste and rejection of downstream and upstream milk is reduced, thus mitigating income loss and GHG emission intensities. Rehabilitation of defective segments of feeder roads for a total of 140 km will improve milk collection and MCCs/MCPs accessibility all year round. The project will support the participatory identification and rehabilitation of defective segments representing approximately 10% of an average 10 km around 140 MCC. These segments will be selected on the basis of the District Road management system (DROMAS), on condition that the permanent link is affected either between MCCs and offtakers or MCPs and MCCs. MoUs will be signed with Tanzania Rural and Urban Road Agency (TARURA) and Zanzibar Road Agency (ZANROAD) to plan, procure and supervise road works (spot improvement and removal of bottlenecks in prioritized collection points). Climate change will pose more risks for water-related damages to roads. The Green Roads for Water (GR4W) approach will be adopted to transform the way roads are built and maintained, by incorporating water management and climate change adaptation in the design and construction of roads. GR4W is a simple approach which yields a triple win: (i) reduction of water related damage to the roads; (ii) minimising adverse impacts of roads on the surrounding landscape; and (iii) managing water for the benefit of roadside water users.  Digitalization of value chain will support off-takers and cooperatives managing MCCs to improve timely payments to farmers, traceability of the quality of milk and linkage to advisory services where farmers might need advisory interventions and access to finance. The project will build the capacity of milk aggregators/cooperatives to improve their record-keeping and management through a digital MCC management information system (MIS) that will: (i) record the production of farmers, (ii) track milk volumes and quality, (iii) manage records of farmer payments promoting the digitalization of transactions which can support de-risk access to finance through credit worthiness and profiling. The project will build a few pilot MCCs capacity to use MIS in coordination with producers/off-takers to facilitate qualitybased payments. The project will also capacitate the Tanzania Dairy Board (TDB) to centralise milk data collection. Subcomponent 2.2 Support to emergence of safe, short and green value chains and milk consumption Small-scale processing generates substantial benefits, in terms of product affordability, job creation, women and youth inclusion, while preserving food safety. Support to small and medium scale processing and safe milk outlets: the project will support the creation of small and medium scale processing units ranging from 500 to 10 000 litres per day. The Project will provide business development services to develop business plans and strengthen management capacities (initial training and continuous coaching) to both collective (including women groups), and individual ventures. The creation of improved milk outlets like milk zones/bars and milk ATMs will also be supported. Youth entrepreneurship across the sector as detailed in the above sections will be supported through specialised youth incubation and training centres[39]. The already deployed software Rural invest provides a strong entry point to work with. Efficient and renewable energy for milk cooling and small-scale processing for decarbonization of the value chain will be promoted: by leveraging GCF climate finance, the project will focus on resource efficiency and the substitution of fossil fuels and firewood by green energy sources such as solar or less wood-intensive energy sources for milk cooling and processing, as well as management of waste and waste water in particular. Support to milk consumption and nutrition awareness will increase availability, accessibility and affordability of quality and safe dairy products, accompanied by nutrition education and social behaviour change and communication to improve their consumption amongst nutritionally vulnerable groups. The project will support market outlets supplying fresh and quality safety dairy for primary school children. National milk consumption promotion campaigns will be implemented at different levels, including schools. Nutrition education will be embedded as part of extension and L-FFS, and nutrition sensitization will include all value chain actors. Training of dairy technologists: the Livestock Training Agency (LITA) provides training at Diploma and Certificate levels for Animal Health and Production technicians but has no curriculum for dairy technologists. The project will support LITA to develop a new specialized curriculum, training of trainers, and roll out the programme. Subcomponent 2.3: Access to financial services facilitation of access to credit: as several financial institutions (FIs) have an appetite for the dairy sector, the project will partner with TADB to leverage its existing instruments including the Smallholder Credit Guarantee Scheme (SCGS), wholesale lending at concessional terms, and technical assistance to its partners financing institutions, to incentivize them to finance the Project target groups. 
In addition and in complementarity with above interventions, the project will also facilitate linkages with ARCAFIM and PADNET, which are expected to provide access to credit lines to FIs for climate adaptation investments for dairy farmers and MSMEs, as well as technical assistance. Subcomponent 2.4. Policy support and stakeholder dialogue, the project will support MLF and MAINL for the formulation and update of national policies, strategies and legislations that are needed for the development and transformation of the sector (including privatization of veterinary services). Where the GoT requires additional expertise or assistance to update, formulate and prepare policies and legislations in a timely manner, support will be given through provision of expertise when needed, facilitation of stakeholder consultations to ensure that the policy dialogue is inclusive enough, and formulation of policy notes to inform policy makers. The main implementing partner for this activity will be FAO, but other partners such as ILRI or other CGIAR institutions could be mobilized to generate the knowledge and data required for informed and evidence-based policy development. These activities the Livestock Sector Transformation Plan and Livestock policy (for dissemination, as drafts are already available), the review of the Animal Health Act (2003) especially on aspects related to private practitioners, the formulation of disease contingency and control plans, the formulation of a Dairy strategy, and a review of the Dairy Act (Regulations on raw milk trade). In Zanzibar, the
project will also provide support for the revision of Zanzibar Livestock Policy (2011), formulation of Zanzibar Livestock Strategic plan and finalization of Zanzibar Animal Resource Management Act, (1999). These already identified policy activities will be implemented during the first half of the project and prioritized to enable smooth implementation of sequential project activities.C-SDTP being a climate smart project can contribute to Tanzania and Zanzibar’s climate change policies and agreements (e.g. NDCs) and include impact measurement (e.g. with tools such as GLEAM-i). Finally, the project will support feasibility studies to provide guidance for policy formulation on demand when needs arise. Two areas related to animal health have already been pre-identified (i) private veterinary care services and (ii) veterinary laboratories.

projects.name: Support the implementation of sustainable fishing practises, and protection of important fish habitats (Enhanced productivity of fisheries) (part AFDP)
projects.description:
Support sustainable fisheries and aquaculture development in Tanzania mainland and Zanzibar government’s strategic objective of promoting sustainable fish production systems from both capture fisheries and aquaculture. The AFDP Programme’s interventions under this subcomponent supports the livelihoods of 18,000 artisanal fishers, 6,000 fish farmers and 15,000 seaweed producers who are dependent on fisheries and aquaculture. More specifically, the investments will result into (i) increased fish production and productivity; (ii) increased and sustainable income for fisher-folks; (iii) Improved nutrition as a result of increased consumption of fish and fish products; (iv) Increased access the recommended gears suitable for sustainable fishing, ideally to replace destructive gears and aiming to reduce the fishing effort; v) enhanced use of selective fishing practices by the use of Fish Aggregating Devices (FADS); and vi) improved utilization of catch and reduce post-harvest losses.
The programme supports the development of a semi-commercial fishing joint venture through 4Ps’ arrangements between the respective government fishing agencies in Tanzania Mainland (TAFICO) and Zanzibar (ZAFICO), private sector investors and small-scale fishers’ cooperative societies. The Programme will finance the acquisition four  fully equipped long line fishing vessels. An integrated fish processing plant will be designed and equipped with modern technologies to meet the regional and international market standards. AFDP will promotes 4P joint-venture shareholding schemes or supply-based arrangements as a mechanism to include smallholder fishers and fish traders in deep sea fishing and fish processing plants. Between 30-40 percent of the catch is expected to be used in the domestic markets through small scale fishers and other actors involved in 15/31 the fishery value chain including youths and women. On the other hand, small scale fishers will supply bait to the vessels which require sufficient amount of baits during its operations. These investments will generate employment directly and indirectly for about 1 000 youth along the tuna value chain, and will provide services and market outlets to over 15,000 artisanal fishers and their cooperative societies to supply fish and baits. AFDP will intervene through developing the capacity of Aquaculture Development Centers (ADCs) (Kingolwira, Mwamapuli and Rubambagwe) to supply high quality Tilapia and catfish seeds and deliver effective extension services. The programme targets to raise the level of Tilapia fingerlings production to an additional 25 million fingerlings, and 10 million of catfish per year at the end of the six-year investment period. Fresh-water aquaculture interventions under AFDP will focuses on: (i) rehabilitating/developing the basic infrastructure for hatchery production (including water supply systems, access roads, hatchery facilities, feed mill and equipment etc.) in three ADCs (Kingolwira, Mwamapuli and Rubambagwe); (ii) developing the Kinglowira ADC to become a breeding nucleus which will produce quality broodstock to be multiplied in other ADCs and private hatcheries for mass production of fingerlings; (iii) establishing and strengthening aquaculture clusters targeting about 6,000 aquafarmers; and (iv) developing a national aquaculture information system. The Programme adopts a cluster growth model, through which the ADCs will nurture and support growth of private hatcheries and aquaculture service providers. AFDP will invest in (i) carrying out tissue culture and micro-propagation technologies to produce at least one ton annually of cottonii to be multiplied in farmers plots; (ii) promoting of new seaweed production methods supporting about 15 000 women farmers to more deeper waters where E. cottonii farming can successfully be undertaken; and (iii) improving and intensifying the cultivation of E. spinosum to increase current production from 400Kg to up to 1.6 tons per farmer annually, increasing farm size from the current 50 ropes units to on average 400 ropes units per farmer; and (iv) training of over 1,000 youth on mariculture in Zanzibar. The programme will finance the rehabilitation and equipment of ZARI laboratory facilities for tissue culture micro-propagation, field testing and large scale on farm multiplication by trained farmers, small boats and hand pulled plastic barges and /hand pulled for women groups and cooperatives.

projects.name: Strengthened on-farm use of climate-resilient varieties and management practices (Enhanced productivity of crop seeds) (part of AFDP)
projects.description:
Crop seed systems development to ensure suitable supply and access to quality seed of adapted productive varieties of maize, sunflower and beans/pulses, to feed smallholder innovation use for more productive and climate-resilient food and market production systems for selected crop value chains in the target areas. To strengthen more efficient seed systems with adequate and sustainable funding, the programme contributes to strengthen key functions of seed value chains (pre-basic, basic and certified seed classes) to enable a sustainable annual offer of quality certified seeds for mainly Open-Pollinated Varieties (OPV), adapted to the demand and based on farming systems sustainability and resilience.
To this end, the programme supports these five priority areas: National seed demand and supply coordination. The Programme provides targeted support to the Ministry of Agriculture (MoA) and the Tanzania Seed Traders Association (TASTA) to enhance: (i) continued update for future seed demand and supply planning (ii) broaden user awareness/information on quality seed use and varieties adapted to agro-ecological zones and consumer/market preferences; (iii) strengthen seed production and distribution networks (including PPs) driven by market and smallholder farmer needs (iv) streamline partner functions, follow-up and propose policy innovations (fight counterfeit seeds); and (iv) facilitate professional seed producers (individuals, cooperatives, upgraded QDS producers) access to adapted technical information and financial products and services, etc., contributing towards sustainable seed systems. Innovation development and Early Generation Seed production. AFDP provides targeted support to TARI for adaptive research and targeted breeding/selection programmes towards: (i) developing productive and climate-risk resilient varieties for the arid and semi-arid agro-ecological zone; and (ii) supply of early generation seeds (EGS), including maintenance/purification of breeder lines and the production of pre-basic seeds to meet the future demand (varieties and quantities) of seed multiplication companies and seed farmers in the target area for maize, sunflower and beans/pulses. Special attention is given to participative selection of improved varieties (mainly OPV but also adapted resilient hybrids adapted to target agro-ecological and farming conditions of vulnerable farmers, prioritizing traits such as high and resilient productivity/yields, tolerance to pests and diseases, improved nutrient composition and consumer acceptance, and adaptation to climate variability and change conditions. As a means of improving TARI performance and outcomes, AFDP supports investment in: (i) upgrading facilities for EGS (breeder and pre-basic seed) production, including irrigation facilities (2 pivot irrigation systems for a total of 25 ha), farm and seed post-harvest equipment, seed storage facilities, scientific/laboratory equipment, field vehicles for research in TARI Ilonga/Kilosa (maize and sunflower) and Seliani/Arusha (maize and beans/pulses); (ii) strengthening institutional capacity and technical expertise in maize, sunflower and bean/pulses varietal improvement and innovative production practices (i.e. CSA); (iii) research costs for strategic breeding and participative varietal selection activities; (iv) enhancing scientific collaboration with regional and international knowledge centers, especially in germplasm access and market-oriented seed systems development; (v) promotion and awareness (pre-vulgarization) of improved varieties and technologies; and (vi) strengthening emerging partnerships between TARI and private seed producers/companies, including for variety licensing. Basic seed multiplication. AFDP supports the Agricultural Seed Agency (ASA)[35] to play its relay role in high quality basic seed multiplication for preferred maize, sunflower and beans/pulses varieties. This step uses TARI supplied pre basic material (mainly OPV) adapted to cropping systems of the target zone to feed the next step of further multiplication in the subsequent year (see bulking up certified seed) towards responding to the demand of the farming community for certified seeds in the target area. As a means of improving ASA performance and sustainable production of basic seeds (in response to demand), AFDP supports targeted investment for strengthening physical, technical and management capacities towards building sustainable seed systems, including: (i) securing annual basic seed production by upgrading/completing of irrigation infrastructures[36] for not exceeding 100 ha each in ASA farms at Msimba (Kilosa/Morogoro) and Kilimi (Nzenga); (ii) construction and/or upgrading of selected seed farm work facilities (seed stores, dry shed, garage facilities, farm offices, field residential and training facilities); (iii) renewing of targeted field production equipment (adapted implements for land preparation, seeding, plant protection and harvesting); (iv) supplying required seed processing treatment plant at both farms; (v) transport equipment for field supervision and seed transport; and (vi) capacity strengthening in seed production and treatment, business development and monitoring and evaluation. 14/31 Bulking-up certified seed. The next step of the seed value chain is the bulking-up of basic seed (produced mainly by ASA) to avail certified seed for distribution/sale to users in the target area and respond to local producer’s needs (renewed every 3 years). Based on current production levels, the production levels of different seed classes will progressively increase in quantities (increase of 5 percent in Y1, 15 percent in Y2 and 25 percent in following years) to reach the targeted annual seed production levels for certified (Year n), basic (Year n-1) and pre-basic seed (Year n-2). Overall, certified seed availability for the target area is expected to reach a sustainable annual certified seed production levels of 7500 MT maize, 3000 MT sunflower, 2000 MT beans and 500 MT pulses by year 6. Simultaneous to availed seed quantities, proposed varieties will adapt gradually to smallholder preferences for food, adaptation to local farming systems, and market requirements (including 10-15 percent for hybrid varieties). AFDP will support ASA to facilitate innovative productive PPPs in close collaboration with TASTA, towards increased private sector participation in the seed industry development by: supporting (matching grants registered private seed enterprises and/or seed farmer cooperatives, to include: (i) supply of quality basic seed (adapted varieties and quantities) for a period of 2 years; (ii) providing specialized technical and management support services and training for seed production and processing of certified seed (in close collaboration with regional MoA and TOSCI officers); (iii) enabling full implementation of the certification process by TOSCI; (iii) facilitating, where possible, partnerships and commercial agreements with private seed producers/SMEs to use ASA facilities (land, irrigation); (iv) payment of initial certification operations at the level of 100 percent, 75 percent, 50 percent and 25 percent respectively in year 1 to 4; and (v) facilitating seed treatment support services at cost (sorting, treating packing, etc.). Seed quality control and certification. AFDP will provide targeted support to Tanzania Official Seed Certification Institute (TOSCI) for strengthening its role in seed quality control and certification, to ensure availability of quality seed of improved varieties to farming communities, while also implementing Distinctness, Uniformity and Stability and National Performance Trials testing of new varieties prior to the integration into the official national crop variety catalogue. As a means of improving TOSCI’s performance and sustainability in supplying regulatory services for the seed sector outcomes, AFDP is supporting investment in: (i) upgrading operational and laboratory facilities at the National seed testing laboratory (Morogoro) and zonal levels (NO-Arusha, NW-Mwanza) including infrastructure rehabilitation and equipment; (ii) enhancing technical and management capacities of seed inspectors, samplers and analysts; (ii) strengthening seed quality control and certification procedures and guidelines; (iii) promoting third party seed certification and data management and build a cadre of private (young and female preference) seed inspectors; (iv) rolling-out of e-tags for digitized authentication of quality seeds by farmers and reduce fake seeds (in collaboration with other partners); and (v) enhancing overall technical and management/business capacities of TOSCI at national and regional levels.

projects.name: Build technical capacities of value chain actors for efficient and inclusive sunflower, maize, beans, and fishery value chains in Tanzania (AFDP)
projects.description:
Support to strengthen sunflower, maize, beans, and fishery value chain in Tanzania. i) designed to enhance market access, value addition, and private sector development for smallholder farmers. Its core strategy revolves around improving the seed business and fish market systems, with a strong emphasis on sustainable agricultural practices and inclusive growth. The programme aims to increase the use of quality seeds by supporting a sustainable supply of locally adapted and climate-resilient varieties. This effort targets 25% of local farming activities, enabling farmers to replace open-pollinated varieties every three years while building their capacity to maintain seed quality. To achieve its goals, AFDP focuses on four strategic areas. First, it establishes regional multi-stakeholder innovation platforms that bring together public, private, and associative actors. These platforms coordinate seed demand and supply, promote climate-smart agriculture, and support the development of professional seed producer and distributor organizations. They also facilitate annual stakeholder meetings and use digital tools for planning and monitoring seed-related activities. Second, the programme strengthens the supply and accessibility of improved seeds by developing agro-dealer networks and village input shops, particularly those managed by women and youth. It promotes partnerships between local agro-dealers and national seed producers, supports group purchases of seeds and inputs, and disseminates technical information through demonstrations and printed materials. Digital technologies are leveraged to enhance seed marketing and facilitate purchases by smallholder farmers.
Third, AFDP promotes farmer awareness and demand for improved seeds. It aims to reach 200,000 households across 40 districts in 10 regions, focusing on maize, sunflower, and pulses. Through farmer field schools, on-farm demonstrations, seed fairs, and nutrition education, the programme introduces farmers to new technologies and best practices. It also empowers local farmer organizations to provide advisory services and uses digital platforms to disseminate information. Financial services are facilitated to support input purchases.
Finally, the programme strengthens market linkages by fostering partnerships between farmers and agribusinesses. It encourages contract farming and pricing agreements with processors, connects farmers to structured trading platforms like G-Soko, and conducts market mapping studies. Support is also provided to youth entrepreneurs and cooperatives, and technical and business information is widely shared. AFDP collaborates with existing initiatives such as the Agricultural Market Development Trust (AMDT) and the Pan African Bean Research Alliance (PABRA) to maximize impact and promote best practices.

ii) The AFDP programme’s fish market development and value addition component focuses on reducing postharvest losses and increasing income opportunities, particularly for women and youth. It aims to improve infrastructure and introduce technologies that enhance the quality and marketability of fish products. These investments are expected to benefit over 30,000 artisanal fishers, processors, and traders, while creating direct and indirect employment for around 1,000 youth along the tuna value chain.
To achieve this, the programme will co-finance the establishment of eight ice-making plants, three cold chain and processing facilities, ten solar dryers for seaweed and small pelagic fish (dagaa), and 80 dagaa drying racks. Additionally, modern fish markets will be rehabilitated in Pangani and Bagamoyo, modeled after successful markets in Dar es Salaam. These facilities will be managed by cooperatives and small enterprises, with sustainable user-fee systems to ensure proper maintenance and long-term viability.
AFDP will also support access to finance for fishers’ cooperatives and associations through partnerships with financial institutions, facilitated by the Tanzania Agricultural Development Bank (TADB). This will enable investment in equipment, infrastructure, and working capital, with a focus on youth and women-led groups.
In aquaculture, the programme will strengthen farmer clusters and link them with private hatcheries. It will establish aquaculture field schools to train youth and women, promote collective marketing, and improve access to inputs and cold storage. These clusters will coordinate production to ensure a steady supply of fish and engage in local governance and policy advocacy.
For the seaweed sector, which is predominantly female-led, AFDP will address challenges in processing and value addition. It will fund market analyses, strengthen cooperatives, and provide equipment such as drying racks, solar dryers, milling machines, and packaging materials. The programme will also support the development of seaweed-based small enterprises and link them to financial and business services. Partnerships with organizations like The Nature Conservancy and buyers such as Cargill will help scale market access and improve product quality. An inclusive business model from Zanzibar will be adapted to Pemba and mainland Tanzania to promote fair pricing, compliance with standards, and collective bargaining.

children.description:
During the reporting period, in March 2022 the mainland Government reviewed and updated the national social protection policy and implementing strategy. The Government conducted five consultations with  different stakeholders from social assistance; social security; productive inclusion and social insurances.  Currently a cabinet paper has been drafted to be submitted to the cabinet. 
The mid-term review of the  productive social safety net program was successfully carried out in January 2022. PSSN II has expanded coverage from 70 percent to 100 percent to all villages and Shehia in mainland and Zanzibar with an estimated 5,180,684  beneficiaries of which 55.7 percent were females and 44.3 percent were males. The total number of households is 1,375,107.  PSSN II impact evaluation design was completed, and the survey questionnaire developed. A total of 434 villages from 32 PAAs were sampled for the evaluation. Training of enumerators on questionnaire management was done and completed and enumerators deployed to conduct data collection in sampled areas.  Total of 60,779 beneficiaries out of 97,430 were found with high level of disability and confirmed as being eligible for disability benefit and  45,875 disability beneficiaries were paid during the  July/August payment period in 2022.
